newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-SACCHI EAGER TO BE BACK AT AC MILAN.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SACCHI EAGER TO BE BACK AT AC MILAN.

text.p: Arrigo Sacchi said on Monday he was eager to return to AC Milan after five years as Italy's national coach, a job in which he increasingly had been seen as a lame duck.
Sacchi told a news conference the decision to return to league soccer had come easily.
"Milan asked me, I accepted with pleasure because I found it difficult to say no to a team which has given me so much," he said. "So I come here with pleasure and enthusiasm."
His new contract runs until the end of the 1997-98 season.

Sacchi, 50, ended months of debate about his future when he called the Italian soccer federation (FIGC) special commissioner Raffaele Pagnozzi shortly before midnight on Sunday to advise him of his decision.
The FIGC said in a statement on Monday evening that it had accepted Sacchi's resignation.
"I think that we have made the right choice by turning to Arrigo Sacchi," billionaire media mogul Silvio Berlusconi, owner of the Italian champions, said on Monday.
Sacchi, who spent five glorious years at Milan until his appointment to the national side in 1991, replaces Oscar Washington Tabarez who has had a bleak six months with the club.
A 3-2 defeat by lowly Piacenza on Sunday dropped Milan, who have a key European Champions' League match against Norway's Rosenborg on Wednesday, to ninth in the league.
About 100 Milan fans, who had waited for hours in cold weather, applauded Sacchi's arrival at the club's headquarters.
He thanked everyone with whom he had worked as Italy's coach, which he called "an important experience", but seemed more interested in talking about his future with Milan.
"Now returning to this adventure, I have come home to the people who always respected me," said Sacchi.
Tabarez was the third serie A coach to leave clubs this season and the second Uruguayan casualty.

It was not yet clear who would succeed Sacchi in the most criticised job in Italian soccer but two men have emerged as clear favourites for the nomination, expected after the FIGC elects a new chairman on December 14.
Italy's next match is away to England in February in a key qualifier for the 1998 World Cup.

Former World Cup-winning goalkeeper Dino Zoff, now chairman of Lazio, has been heavily tipped as a likely replacement despite a nondescript coaching record. Under-21 coach Cesare Maldini has been seen as a possible stop-gap but he declined to comment on Sacchi's job change.
Former Parma coach Nevio Scala is immediately available having left his club at the end of last season.

Other candidates, seemingly more from the realms of fantasy football than reality, included Bayern Munich coach Giovanni Trappatoni and Real Madrid's Fabio Capello, who replaced Sacchi as Milan coach in 1991. But both said they were not interested.
Sacchi took Italy to the 1994 World Cup final in Los Angeles, where they lost on penalties to Brazil, but has been under intense pressure since the side crashed out of Euro 96 in the first phase.
His last match in charge was a friendly against Bosnia in Sarajevo last month that Italy lost 2-1.
He has been criticised for frequent change -- trying out almost 100 players in five years -- and falling out with key men, most notably Gianluca Vialli of Chelsea.
Soft-spoken, reserved and with his sunglasses almost permanently perched on his forehead, Sacchi divided Italy. Some disliked him so much that they formed an anti-Sacchi club.
Sacchi said he was willing to join, too.
